title: Multi-region egress routing playbook
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures a pragmatic design for multi-region traffic steering for Redwood Inference control plane and egress API endpoints. Goal: minimize user-visible latency, preserve SLOs during region outages, and keep per-token cost predictable. Target audiences: platform engineers, infra, SRE, and anyone implementing routing policies for hosted API, dedicated frontdoors, and private control planes.

Key constraints we must respect:
- Some customers pin traffic to specific regions (compliance/latency).
- Regional capacity may vary (GPU constraints) so routing must support dynamic weight adjustments and graceful degradation.
- Control plane must be resilient to split-brain or partial control-plane outages.
- DNS TTLs, Anycast convergence, and client-side caching create different failure/steering behaviors — design must account for each.

High-level approach (hybrid steering):
We recommend a layered steering model rather than a single mechanism:
1) Primary steering: low-TTL Geo-aware DNS (GeoDNS) for long-lived affinity and coarse region preference.
2) Fast failover & global front door: Anycasted any-region edge for instant ingress and health-probed routing to origin (regional pools).
3) Intra-edge steering: per-request regional preference and weighted routing via control-plane policy API.
4) Fallback: client-controlled region hints and transparent cross-region proxying when allowed.

Why hybrid?
- GeoDNS is cheap and widely supported and gives good default locality; but changes take TTL to propagate and client OS resolvers can cache longer than TTL.
- Anycast reduces failover time (BGP convergence) and supports steady-state global frontdoors. But it can hide origin region among multiple POPs and complicate region affinity and source-IP geography checks.
- A control-plane-aware edge (global front door) lets us make per-request decisions (weighted, canary, capacity-aware) and roll out policies quickly without waiting for DNS.

Design components and responsibilities:
1) GeoDNS layer:
- Purpose: initial region selection, compliance locality, and predictable baseline traffic distribution.
- Implementation: use managed GeoDNS (e.g., AWS Route 53 geolocation + latency-based routing) with configurable default regions per customer account and an override map in the control plane.
- TTL: default 30s for endpoints where we expect quicker changes; 300s for privacy-sensitive or compliance critical customers. Must allow per-customer override.
- Health signals: GeoDNS health checks driven by global health aggregator (SRE job). When a region is marked unhealthy, GeoDNS removes it from the pool for affected prefixes.

2) Anycast edge + regional origin pools:
- Purpose: minimize user-visible failover, reduce handshake latency, and pre-warm client connections.
- Anycast behavior: advertise same frontdoor IPs from multiple POPs. Edge accepts requests and routes to an origin region pool via internal routing/consistent hashing.
- Sticky session approach: use token-affinity cookie or authorization token mapping to preferred origin region stored in KV cache at edge. If affinity is unknown, consult control-plane policy API (fast cacheable).
- Health checks: edge pulls health status and regional capacity metadata; failing regions are drained asynchronously.

3) Control plane policy API:
- Purpose: single source of truth for routing policies (customer-level preferences, rollouts, cost-based routing).
- API semantics: GET /routing-policy/{customer} returns ordered list: [region-preferences], weights, sticky rules, allowed-fallback-regions, and max-cost-per-token. Values are small and cachable for X seconds (default 5s).
- Conflict resolution: local customer policy overrides org defaults; operator overrides for emergencies. All policy changes are versioned and rollouts support canary scope.

4) Failure and failover modes:
- Soft degradation (preferred): when origin latency rises but region still responsive, edge can route a percentage of traffic to secondary regions based on weights.
- Hard failover: region marked unhealthy -> GeoDNS and control-plane remove region for new resolutions/routing; edge drains connections and returns 503 for region-specific pinned customers unless fallback is allowed.
- Data locality exceptions: for customers with strict data residency, disallow cross-region fallback; return explicit error and guidance.

Routing policy primitives (for policy authors):
- region_preference: ordered list (primary, secondary...)
- weight_map: region -> percent for split-traffic
- failover_mode: immediate | gradual | none
- ttl_hint: seconds for GeoDNS
- allow_cross_region_proxy: true|false
- max_burst_rps_per_region: integer
- cost_target_usd_per_million_tokens: decimal

Control-plane to edge protocol considerations:
- Polling vs push: hybrid. Edges keep local cache; control plane pushes critical changes via long-lived multiplexed connection (gRPC stream) for urgent failovers. Non-urgent updates pulled via short TTL (5s) REST fetch to avoid controlling data plane churn.
- Edge cache invalidation: support versioned policy objects with monotonic increment to detect missed pushes and trigger full refetch.
- Backoff behavior: if control-plane unreachable, edge must rely on last-known policy and, after a configurable staleness window, fall back to a safe global default policy.

GeoDNS specifics and caveats:
- Many client resolvers (mobile carriers, corporate resolvers) ignore low TTLs. Consider application-layer health checks and edge-level steering to correct suboptimal DNS choices.
- GeoIP accuracy: maintain a curated list of IP ranges for major cloud providers; allow manual override for major customer hubs.
- Split-horizon for compliance: customers with residency constraints get a separate host (regional-only DNS record) to avoid misrouting by global DNS.

Anycast-specific caveats:
- BGP blackholing during prefix withdraws can cause transient packet loss across many users; coordinate withdraws carefully and only after edge drain procedures.
- Origin selection post-anycast: prefer origin selection based on both region_preference and origin health; avoid pure shortest-AS-path heuristics when origin capacity is limited.

Operational playbook (day-to-day):
- On normal days: GeoDNS handles most traffic; edges honor policies and metrics flow to console.
- On capacity pressure: control-plane triggers weight adjustments to throttle regions; console shows per-region headroom and estimated cost delta.
- On partial regional outage: 1) Mark region degraded in health aggregator 2) Push emergency routing policy via gRPC to edges 3) Rebalance GeoDNS after 60s 4) Notify customers pinned to region with recommended actions 5) Open incident on severity timeline.

Testing and validation:
- Chaos tests: automated regularly scheduled tests that simulate regional BGP withdraw and origin slowdowns. Verify Anycast convergence and policy push reliability.
- Synthetic clients in major markets to measure end-to-end effect of GeoDNS change (time to shift to new region) and to estimate resolver caching anomalies.
- Canary rollout of policy changes: run 1% traffic through new weight_map before scaling.

Observability signals to surface:
- Per-region latency P95/P99, error-rate, capacity headroom, token-cost-per-region, and DNS resolution distribution.
- Edge policy staleness metric (time since last successful policy refresh).
- Number of requests served where GeoDNS region != origin region (useful to detect resolver inconsistency).

Security and compliance notes:
- Ensure policies that permit cross-region failover are visible in the customer UI and require an explicit opt-in for residency-restricted accounts.
- Audit logs: every routing policy change must be logged with actor, timestamp, and diffs. Retention per enterprise agreement.

Migration plan (how to roll this in):
1) Implement policy API and edge caching primitives in a branch; add read-only console views for policies.
2) Launch Anycast edge in 3 pilot POPs and enable read-only routing decisions (no GeoDNS change).
3) Run shadow mode for 2 weeks where policy decisions are recorded but not enforced; analyze mismatches.
4) Flip active enforcement for a small subset of customers (beta).
5) Gradually expand and start GeoDNS TTL tuning and split-horizon DNS for residency customers.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Rollout timeouts for BGP withdraw coordination: what is our max tolerable blackhole window? (ops input needed)
- Cost-sensitivity hooks: should control-plane automatically re-route to cheaper regions when cost exceeds threshold or require explicit opt-in?
- Exact TTL defaults per customer tier — security/compliance teams to provide constraints for enterprise customers.

Action items (owners):
- (Priya) Draft control-plane API schema and versioning model.
- (Diego) Prototype edge policy caching and gRPC push channel.
- (Lina) Run GeoDNS resolver experiments across 10 carrier networks and report caching behavior.
- (Markus) Draft BGP withdraw playbook with SRE and network partners.

Appendix: example policy JSON (example for humans)
{ region_preference: ["us-west-2", "us-east-1"], weight_map: {us-west-2: 90, us-east-1: 10}, failover_mode: "gradual", ttl_hint: 30, allow_cross_region_proxy: true }

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally pragmatic and operationally focused — want feedback on control-plane to edge latency guarantees, acceptable TTL behavior, and how strict we need to be for residency-locked customers.

End of document.
